claim: MYPN is a striated muscle-specific immunoglobulin domain-containing protein located in the sarcomeric Z-line and I-band.
source: Myopalladin (MYPN) is a striated muscle-specific immunoglobulin domain-containing protein located in the sarcomeric Z-line and I-band.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a background statement about MYPN.

claim: MYPN gene mutations are causative for dilated (DCM), hypertrophic, and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
source: MYPN gene mutations are causative for dilated (DCM), hypertrophic, and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: MYPN was found to bind to titin in the Z-line in a yeast two-hybrid screening.
source: In a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) screening of a skeletal muscle cDNA library using titin Ig domains Z4-Z5 in the titin Z-line region as a bait, we identified MYPN as an interaction partner (Figure 1A)
evidence: The manuscript describes a Y2H screening experiment that identified MYPN as binding to titin Z4-Z5, with results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The interaction between MYPN and titin Z4-Z5 was confirmed by microscale thermophoresis.
source: MYPN was found to bind to titin in the Z-line, which was confirmed by microscale thermophoresis.
evidence: The abstract states that the Y2H finding was confirmed by MST, and detailed MST data are presented in the results.

claim: The MYPN C-terminal region from residue 935 to 1320 binds to titin Ig domains Z4-Z5.
source: We subsequently narrowed down the interaction site to the MYPN C-terminal region from residue 935 to 1320, containing its three C-terminal Ig domains.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the Y2H experiments.

claim: PALLD binds to titin Ig domains Z4-Z5.
source: The corresponding region in its homologue PALLD (Res. 794–1123; Acc. NM_001166108) likewise bound to titin.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) for MYPN C-terminal binding to titin Z4-Z5 was estimated to 2.8 ± 0.5 μM.
source: Under this experimental condition, full binding saturation was achieved and the Kd was estimated to 2.8 ± 0.5 μM (Figure 1C).
evidence: MST binding experiments were performed and the Kd was calculated from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The C-terminal region of MYPN and PALLD bind to titin Ig domains Z4-Z5 with apparent affinities in the low micromolar range.
source: This revealed that the C-terminal region of MYPN as well as the homologous PALLD region bind to the titin Ig domains Z4-Z5 with apparent affinities in the low micromolar range, comparable to other Z-line scaffold complexes (e.g. the interaction between titin Z-repeats and ACTN2), which have Kd values between 100 nM and 4 μM (Joseph et al., 2001).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MST data and compared to published values for other Z-line interactions.

claim: MKO mice are born at Mendelian ratios and have a normal life span.
source: As previously reported, MKO mice are born at Mendelian ratios and have a normal life span (Filomena et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to a previous publication.

claim: Histological analyses revealed no histological abnormalities in MKO mouse hearts up to 6 months of age.
source: Histological analyses by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of hearts from wild-type (WT) and MKO mice revealed no histological abnormalities up to 6 months of age
evidence: H&E staining results are described in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MKO mice showed no evidence of fibrosis, necrosis, or myofibrillar disarray up to 6 months of age.
source: Picro Sirius Red stainings showed no evidence of fibrosis, necrosis, or myofibrillar disarray in WT and MKO mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Picro Sirius Red staining results are described and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TUNEL staining showed no signs of apoptosis in MKO mice.
source: Furthermore, TUNEL staining showed no signs of apoptosis (data not shown).
evidence: TUNEL staining was performed but data are not shown.

claim: Cardiomyocyte length is similar in WT and MKO mice at 4 months of age.
source: Measurements on isolated cardiomyocytes (CMCs) from 4-month-old mice showed similar CMC length in WT and MKO mice (Figure 2B and C)
evidence: CMC measurements were performed and results are shown in Figures 2B and C.

claim: Cardiomyocyte width is significantly reduced in MKO mice at 4 months of age.
source: Measurements on isolated cardiomyocytes (CMCs) from 4-month-old mice showed similar CMC length in WT and MKO mice (Figure 2B and C), but significantly reduced CMC width and size in MKO mice (Figure 2D and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: CMC width measurements were performed and statistical significance is shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: Cardiomyocyte size is significantly reduced in MKO mice at 4 months of age.
source: Measurements on isolated cardiomyocytes (CMCs) from 4-month-old mice showed similar CMC length in WT and MKO mice (Figure 2B and C), but significantly reduced CMC width and size in MKO mice (Figure 2D and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: CMC size measurements were performed and statistical significance is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduced cardiomyocyte size in MKO mice is possibly due to reduced body weight.
source: but significantly reduced CMC width and size in MKO mice (Figure 2D and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), possibly due to reduced body weight of MKO mice (11.8% at 4 months of age; see Figure 3J and Figure 3—source data 2) as previously reported (Filomena et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript speculates that reduced CMC size may be due to reduced body weight, referencing data in Figure 3J and a previous publication.

claim: Body weight is reduced by 11.8% in MKO mice at 4 months of age.
source: possibly due to reduced body weight of MKO mice (11.8% at 4 months of age; see Figure 3J and Figure 3—source data 2) as previously reported (Filomena et al., 2020).
evidence: Body weight reduction is stated with a specific percentage and referenced to Figure 3J.

claim: The body weight to tibia length ratio is reduced in MKO mice.
source: The body weight to tibia length ratio was reduced in MKO mice (Figure 2F)
evidence: The BW/TL ratio was measured and results are shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The lower body weight of MKO mice is mainly due to reduced muscle weight as a result of reduced myofiber cross-sectional area.
source: The body weight to tibia length ratio was reduced in MKO mice (Figure 2F), indicating that the lower body weight of MKO mice is mainly due to reduced muscle weight as a result of the previously reported reduction in myofiber cross-sectional area (Filomena et al., 2020).
evidence: This interpretation is based on the BW/TL ratio data and a previous publication about skeletal muscle phenotype.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy analyses showed normal sarcomere organization in MKO mice at 8 months of age.
source: Transmission electron microscopy analyses of papillary muscle from 8-month-old MKO compared to littermate control mice showed normal sarcomere organization with no alterations in Z-line structure (Figure 2G).
evidence: TEM was performed and images are shown in Figure 2G.

claim: MKO mice showed no alterations in Z-line structure at 8 months of age.
source: Transmission electron microscopy analyses of papillary muscle from 8-month-old MKO compared to littermate control mice showed normal sarcomere organization with no alterations in Z-line structure (Figure 2G).
evidence: TEM analysis of Z-line structure is described and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Intercalated disc structure appeared normal in MKO mice at 8 months of age.
source: Also ICD structure appeared normal
evidence: Visual assessment of ICD structure from TEM images.

claim: ICD fold amplitude is increased by approximately 27% in MKO mice at 8 months of age.
source: but measurement of ICD fold amplitude revealed an ~ 27% increase in MKO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 2H1).
evidence: ICD fold amplitude was measured from TEM images and quantified in Figure 2I.

claim: MKO mice develop mild left ventricular dilation.
source: This revealed mild left ventricular dilation without alteration in left ventricular wall and septum thickness in MKO mice, consistent with eccentric remodeling.
evidence: Echocardiography data shown in Figure 3A-I demonstrate increased LVIDd and LVIDs in MKO mice.

claim: MKO mice show no alteration in left ventricular wall and septum thickness.
source: This revealed mild left ventricular dilation without alteration in left ventricular wall and septum thickness in MKO mice, consistent with eccentric remodeling.
evidence: Echocardiography measurements of LVPW and IVS shown in Figure 3E-F show no significant differences.

claim: MKO mice exhibit eccentric remodeling.
source: This revealed mild left ventricular dilation without alteration in left ventricular wall and septum thickness in MKO mice, consistent with eccentric remodeling.
evidence: The pattern of increased chamber size without increased wall thickness is interpreted as eccentric remodeling.

claim: MKO mice show a reduction in cardiac systolic function.
source: This was associated with a reduction in cardiac systolic function in MKO mice as reflected by a fractional shortening of 30.2% ± 0.4% in MKO mice vs. 40.0% ± 0.4% in WT mice at 4 months of age
evidence: Echocardiography data in Figure 3C show significantly reduced fractional shortening in MKO mice.

claim: Fractional shortening is 30.2% ± 0.4% in MKO mice vs. 40.0% ± 0.4% in WT mice at 4 months of age.
source: This was associated with a reduction in cardiac systolic function in MKO mice as reflected by a fractional shortening of 30.2% ± 0.4% in MKO mice vs. 40.0% ± 0.4% in WT mice at 4 months of age
evidence: Specific fractional shortening values are provided from echocardiography measurements.

claim: MKO mice show a significant reduction in cardiac output at 6 months of age.
source: as well as a significant reduction in cardiac output at 6 months of age (20.9 ± 0.9 in MKO mice vs. 23.4 ± 0.7 in WT mice).
evidence: Cardiac output measurements from echocardiography are shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Heart weight is reduced in MKO mice at 6 months of age.
source: Heart weight was reduced in MKO mice at 6 months of age
evidence: Heart weight measurements are shown in Figure 3K.

claim: There is a trend toward increased heart weight to body weight ratio in MKO mice, which is statistically significant only at 4 months of age.
source: but due to reduced body weight of MKO mice, there was a trend toward increased heart weight to body weight ratio in MKO mice, which, however, was only statistically significant in 4-month-old mice (Figure 3J–L and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: HW/BW ratio data are shown in Figure 3L with statistical analysis.

claim: Maximum Ca2+-activated isometric tension is reduced in MKO myofibrils.
source: Consistent with the reduced cardiac systolic function observed in MKO mice, maximum Ca2+-activated isometric tension was reduced in MKO myofibrils
evidence: Myofibril mechanical measurements are presented in Table 1 showing reduced P0 in MKO.

claim: There are no differences in the kinetics of force generation and relaxation following rapid Ca2+ increase and removal in MKO myofibrils.
source: while there were no differences in the kinetics of force generation and relaxation following rapid Ca2+ increase and removal (Table 1).
evidence: Kinetic parameters (kACT and kREL) in Table 1 show no significant differences between WT and MKO.

claim: The lack of MYPN does not affect myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity.
source: Furthermore, measurements of the tension generated at submaximal (pCa 5.75) vs. maximal (pCa 4.50) Ca2+ activation in Ca2+ jump experiments showed a similar ratio in WT and MKO myofibrils (Figure 3M), providing strong evidence that the lack of MYPN does not affect myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity.
evidence: Ca2+ sensitivity measurements are shown in Figure 3M with no significant difference between WT and MKO.

claim: Resting tension at optimal sarcomere length does not differ between WT and MKO myofibril preparations.
source: The resting tension at optimal sarcomere length also did not differ between WT and MKO preparations (Table 1).
evidence: Resting tension (RT) values in Table 1 show no significant difference.

claim: MKO myofibrils show increased resting tension at sarcomere lengths > 2.20 μm.
source: On the other hand, determination of the sarcomere-length-tension relationship revealed increased resting tension in MKO myofibrils at sarcomere lengths > 2.20 μm (Figure 3N).
evidence: Sarcomere length-tension relationship data are shown in Figure 3N with statistical significance at longer sarcomere lengths.

claim: The passive mechanical properties of cardiac myofibrils are mostly determined by titin.
source: The passive mechanical properties of cardiac myofibrils are mostly determined by titin (Linke and Fernandez, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Titin-based stiffness is regulated by titin isoform expression and posttranslational modifications.
source: Titin-based stiffness is regulated by titin isoform expression (i.e. the ratio between the long and compliant titin N2BA isoform and the shorter and stiffer titin N2B isoform) and posttranslational modifications of the elastic I-band titin region, including phosphorylation and oxidative modifications, such as S-glutathionylation and intramolecular disulfide bond formation and isomerization (Koser et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: No differences in titin isoform expression were observed between WT and MKO mice.
source: However, no differences were observed between WT and MKO mice except for a slight increase in Ser4080 phosphorylation (which reduces passive stiffness) in MKO mice (Figure 3R and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Titin isoform ratio data are shown in Figure 3O with no significant difference.

claim: MKO mice show a slight increase in titin Ser4080 phosphorylation.
source: However, no differences were observed between WT and MKO mice except for a slight increase in Ser4080 phosphorylation (which reduces passive stiffness) in MKO mice (Figure 3R and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Phosphorylation data are shown in Figure 3R with statistical significance.

claim: Ser4080 phosphorylation reduces passive stiffness.
source: However, no differences were observed between WT and MKO mice except for a slight increase in Ser4080 phosphorylation (which reduces passive stiffness) in MKO mice (Figure 3R and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This functional consequence of Ser4080 phosphorylation is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The increased stiffness in MKO myofibrils is not due to increased titin-based stiffness.
source: suggesting that the increased stiffness in MKO myofibrils is not due to increased titin-based stiffness, although it cannot be excluded that titin may be differentially phosphorylated on other sites within its elastic spring elements or subject to oxidative modification.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the titin analysis data, with acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: Both WT and MKO mice showed increased left ventricular wall and septum thickness after TAC.
source: Both WT and MKO mice showed increased left ventricular wall and septum thickness after TAC.
evidence: Echocardiography data in Figure 4E-F show increased LVPW and IVS in both groups after TAC.

claim: WT mice developed compensatory concentric hypertrophy after TAC.
source: However, while, as expected, WT mice developed compensatory concentric hypertrophy
evidence: This is inferred from the echocardiography data showing increased wall thickness without chamber dilation in WT mice.

claim: MKO mice developed eccentric hypertrophy after TAC.
source: MKO mice developed eccentric hypertrophy as indicated by a significantly reduced relative wall thickness, characterized by left ventricular dilation as well as reduced fractional shortening and ejection fraction starting already from 1 week after TAC.
evidence: Echocardiography data in Figure 4 show chamber dilation with reduced RWT and systolic function in MKO mice after TAC.

claim: MKO mice show significantly reduced relative wall thickness after TAC.
source: MKO mice developed eccentric hypertrophy as indicated by a significantly reduced relative wall thickness
evidence: RWT data are shown in Figure 4G with statistical significance.

claim: MKO mice show left ventricular dilation after TAC.
source: characterized by left ventricular dilation as well as reduced fractional shortening and ejection fraction starting already from 1 week after TAC.
evidence: LVIDd and LVIDs data in Figure 4A-B show increased chamber dimensions in MKO mice after TAC.

claim: MKO mice show reduced fractional shortening starting from 1 week after TAC.
source: characterized by left ventricular dilation as well as reduced fractional shortening and ejection fraction starting already from 1 week after TAC.
evidence: Fractional shortening data in Figure 4C show significant reduction in MKO mice at 1 week post-TAC.

claim: MKO mice show reduced ejection fraction starting from 1 week after TAC.
source: characterized by left ventricular dilation as well as reduced fractional shortening and ejection fraction starting already from 1 week after TAC.
evidence: Ejection fraction data in Figure 4D show significant reduction in MKO mice at 1 week post-TAC.

claim: Cardiac output was not affected in MKO mice after TAC.
source: Cardiac output was not affected, likely due to compensatory left ventricular dilation in MKO mice.
evidence: Cardiac output data in Figure 4H show no significant difference between WT and MKO mice after TAC.

claim: The maintained cardiac output in MKO mice after TAC is likely due to compensatory left ventricular dilation.
source: Cardiac output was not affected, likely due to compensatory left ventricular dilation in MKO mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cardiac output data in the context of chamber dilation.

claim: The heart weight to body weight ratio was increased in both WT and MKO mice 4 weeks after TAC.
source: As expected, the heart weight to body weight ratio (Figure 4J–L and Figure 4—source data 1) was increased in both WT and MKO mice 4 weeks after TAC.
evidence: HW/BW ratio data in Figure 4L show significant increases in both groups after TAC.

claim: The heart weight to body weight ratio was significantly higher in MKO mice compared to WT mice after TAC.
source: However, due to reduced body weight of MKO mice, the heart weight to body weight ratio was significantly higher in MKO mice compared to WT mice, although the heart weight was similar in WT and MKO mice.
evidence: HW/BW ratio comparison between WT and MKO after TAC is shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Heart weight was similar in WT and MKO mice after TAC.
source: although the heart weight was similar in WT and MKO mice.
evidence: Heart weight data in Figure 4K show no significant difference between WT and MKO after TAC.

claim: MKO mice showed severe left ventricular dilation 4 weeks after TAC.
source: Histological analyses performed 4 weeks after TAC showed severe left ventricular dilation of MKO mice, often associated with left atrial enlargement (Figure 5A).
evidence: Histological images in Figure 5A show marked chamber dilation in MKO mice after TAC.

claim: MKO mice often showed left atrial enlargement 4 weeks after TAC.
source: Histological analyses performed 4 weeks after TAC showed severe left ventricular dilation of MKO mice, often associated with left atrial enlargement (Figure 5A).
evidence: Histological images in Figure 5A show atrial enlargement in some MKO mice.

claim: Increased interstitial and perivascular fibrosis was observed in MKO mice 4 weeks after TAC.
source: Additionally, increased interstitial and perivascular fibrosis was observed in MKO mice (Figure 5A, middle and Figure 5B).
evidence: Picro Sirius Red staining and quantification in Figure 5A-B show increased fibrosis in MKO mice after TAC.

claim: Cardiomyocyte size increased in both WT and MKO mice 4 weeks after TAC.
source: Measurements of CMC size on wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-stained sections showed increased CMC size in both WT and MKO mice 4 weeks after TAC (Figure 5A, C, D).
evidence: WGA staining and quantification in Figure 5C-D show increased CMC size in both groups after TAC.

claim: Cardiomyocyte size was significantly smaller in MKO mice compared to WT mice both in SHAM- and TAC-operated mice.
source: However, the CMC size was significantly smaller in MKO mice compared to WT mice both in SHAM- and TAC-operated mice, consistent with the results from the analysis of isolated CMCs from 4-month-old mice (Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: CMC size data in Figure 5D show smaller CMCs in MKO mice in both conditions.

claim: MKO mice showed normal sarcomere structure after TAC.
source: Transmission electron microscopy analyses of papillary muscle showed normal sarcomere structure in MKO mice after TAC (Figure 5E).
evidence: TEM images in Figure 5E show normal sarcomere organization.

claim: MKO mice showed an approximately 70% increase in ICD fold amplitude compared to WT mice after TAC.
source: However, MKO mice showed an ~70% increase in ICD fold amplitude compared to WT mice
evidence: ICD fold amplitude quantification in Figure 5G shows significant increase in MKO mice after TAC.

claim: No significant increase in ICD fold amplitude was observed in WT mice after TAC.
source: while no significant increase in ICD fold amplitude was observed in WT mice after TAC (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: ICD fold amplitude data in Figure 5G show no significant change in WT mice after TAC.

claim: MKO mice exhibit progressive moderate cardiac dilation and reduced cardiac systolic function under basal conditions.
source: To summarize, MKO mice exhibit progressive moderate cardiac dilation and reduced cardiac systolic function under basal conditions
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the echocardiography data presented in Figure 3.

claim: MKO mice quickly develop eccentric hypertrophy with severe systolic dysfunction following mechanical pressure overload.
source: and quickly develop eccentric hypertrophy with severe systolic dysfunction following mechanical pressure overload.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the TAC data presented in Figures 4-5.

claim: CARP was highly upregulated after TAC.
source: As expected, CARP (encoded by Ankrd1) was highly upregulated after TAC
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6K show increased CARP protein levels after TAC.

claim: There was no significant difference in CARP protein levels between WT and MKO mice after TAC.
source: but despite increased transcript levels in MKO mice (Figure 6E), there was no significant difference between WT and MKO mice (Figure 6K and M).
evidence: Western blot quantification in Figure 6M shows no significant difference in CARP protein between WT and MKO after TAC.

claim: There were no changes in the activation of Akt and mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathways in MKO mice.
source: Furthermore, there were no changes in the activation of Akt and mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathways (Figure 6K).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6K show no differences in phosphorylation of Akt, Erk1/2, and P38.

claim: CASQ2 levels were increased 4 weeks after TAC in both WT and MKO mice.
source: Western blot analyses for proteins involved in calcium handling revealed increased calsequestrin-2 (CASQ2) levels 4 weeks after TAC in both WT and MKO mice
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6K and N show increased CASQ2 at 4 weeks post-TAC.

claim: CASQ2 levels were significantly reduced in MKO mice compared to WT mice 4 days after TAC.
source: but significantly reduced CASQ2 levels in MKO mice compared to WT mice 4 days after TAC (Figure 6K and N).

claim: Casq2 transcript levels were not significantly changed in WT and MKO mice after TAC.
source: At the transcriptional level, Casq2 was not significantly changed in WT and MKO mice after TAC (Figure 6J)
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 6J show no significant changes in Casq2 mRNA.

claim: CASQ2 is regulated at the post-transcriptional level.
source: suggesting that CASQ2 is regulated at the post-transcriptional level.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the discrepancy between mRNA and protein levels.

claim: The expression of other proteins involved in calcium handling was similar between WT and MKO mice.
source: The expression of other proteins involved in calcium handling was similar between WT and MKO mice (Figure 6K).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6K show no significant differences in SERCA2A, PLN, pPLN, RyR2, pRyR2, NCX, CACNA1C, and CACNA1S.

claim: No significant differences were observed in levels or localization of PALLD or MYPN-interacting proteins.
source: No significant differences were observed in levels (Figure 6K) or localization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) of the MYPN homologue PALLD or MYPN-interacting proteins.
evidence: Western blot and immunofluorescence data show no changes in these proteins.

source: Western blot analysis for components of the ICD, including desmosomal (desmoplakin, plakoglobin/γ-catenin), adherens junction (N-cadherin, α-E-catenin, β-catenin, plakoglobin/γ-catenin, vinculin, sorbin and SH3 domain-containing 2 (SORBS2, also known as Arg-binding protein 2)), and gap junction (connexin 43) proteins, showed upregulation of desmoplakin in MKO vs. WT mice 4 days after TAC (~2.3-fold; Figure 6K and O)

claim: SORBS2 was upregulated in MKO mice under basal conditions by approximately 1.6-fold.

claim: SORBS2 was upregulated in MKO mice at early and late time points after TAC.

evidence: Western blot quantification in Figure 6P shows upregulation of SORBS2 in MKO mice after TAC.

claim: SORBS2 is a known interaction partner of PALLD.
source: while SORBS2, a known interaction partner of PALLD (Rönty et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous publication.

claim: The SORBS2 interaction site in PALLD is located in a proline-rich region not present in MYPN.
source: The SORBS2 interaction site in PALLD is located in a proline-rich region, not present in MYPN (Rönty et al., 2005).

source: No differences in sarcomere shortening were observed between WT and MKO mice

claim: MKO mice show enlargement of the left ventricle under basal conditions.
source: characterized by enlargement of the left ventricle and impaired systolic function without evidence of fibrosis or apoptosis
evidence: Echocardiography data in Figure 3 show increased LVIDd and LVIDs.

claim: MKO mice show impaired systolic function under basal conditions.
source: characterized by enlargement of the left ventricle and impaired systolic function without evidence of fibrosis or apoptosis
evidence: Echocardiography data in Figure 3 show reduced fractional shortening and ejection fraction.

claim: MKO mice show no evidence of fibrosis under basal conditions.
source: characterized by enlargement of the left ventricle and impaired systolic function without evidence of fibrosis or apoptosis
evidence: Picro Sirius Red staining in Figure 2A shows no fibrosis.

claim: MKO mice show no evidence of apoptosis under basal conditions.
source: characterized by enlargement of the left ventricle and impaired systolic function without evidence of fibrosis or apoptosis
evidence: TUNEL staining showed no apoptosis (mentioned in text).

claim: MKO mice showed a slightly increased ICD fold amplitude at the ultrastructural level.
source: At the ultrastructural level, MKO mice showed normal sarcomere organization, but a slightly increased ICD fold amplitude.
evidence: TEM analysis and quantification in Figure 2H-I show increased ICD fold amplitude.

claim: The reduction in force generating capacity in MKO mice is likely due to structural reasons.
source: As MYPN is unlikely to affect the cross-bridge unitary force, the reduction in force generating capacity is likely due to structural reasons.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the myofibril mechanics data and knowledge of MYPN function.

claim: MKO mice rapidly developed maladaptive cardiac remodeling in response to TAC-induced mechanical pressure overload.
source: In response to biomechanical stress by TAC-induced mechanical pressure overload, MKO mice rapidly developed maladaptive cardiac remodeling, characterized by eccentric hypertrophy with left ventricular dilation and severely impaired systolic function (illustrated in Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on all the TAC data presented.

claim: Maladaptive cardiac remodeling in MKO mice after TAC was accompanied by reactivation of the fetal gene program.
source: This was accompanied by reactivation of the fetal gene program and myocardial fibrosis, hallmarks of pathological remodeling and heart failure.
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 6 show upregulation of fetal genes after TAC.

claim: Maladaptive cardiac remodeling in MKO mice after TAC was accompanied by myocardial fibrosis.
source: This was accompanied by reactivation of the fetal gene program and myocardial fibrosis, hallmarks of pathological remodeling and heart failure.
evidence: Picro Sirius Red staining in Figure 5A-B shows increased fibrosis after TAC.

claim: Reactivation of the fetal gene program and myocardial fibrosis are hallmarks of pathological remodeling and heart failure.
source: This was accompanied by reactivation of the fetal gene program and myocardial fibrosis, hallmarks of pathological remodeling and heart failure.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: MKO mice showed more convoluted ICDs compared to WT mice after TAC.
source: Furthermore, MKO mice showed more convoluted ICDs compared to WT mice, an observation frequently associated with DCM (Perriard et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: TEM analysis and quantification in Figure 5F-G show increased ICD fold amplitude in MKO mice after TAC.

claim: More convoluted ICDs are frequently associated with DCM.
source: Furthermore, MKO mice showed more convoluted ICDs compared to WT mice, an observation frequently associated with DCM (Perriard et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous publications.

claim: WT control mice exhibited compensatory cardiac hypertrophy without a major increase in left ventricular internal dimension after TAC.
source: In contrast, WT control mice exhibited compensatory cardiac hypertrophy without a major increase in the left ventricular internal dimension.
evidence: Echocardiography data in Figure 4 show increased wall thickness without significant chamber dilation in WT mice after TAC.

claim: MYPN indirectly binds to the titin N2A region in the I-band through its interaction with CARP.
source: We previously demonstrated that MYPN indirectly binds to the titin N2A region in the I-band through its interaction with CARP (Bang et al., 2001; Miller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous publications by the authors.

claim: MYPN directly binds to the titin Ig domains Z4-Z5 at the Z-line.
source: In the present study, we discovered that MYPN as well as PALLD directly bind to the titin Ig domains Z4-Z5 at the Z-line.
evidence: This is based on the Y2H and MST data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Titin is the largest known protein and stretches from the Z-line to the M-band.
source: Titin is the largest known protein and stretches from the Z-line to the M-band, acting as a molecular spring responsible for passive force in striated muscle and for keeping the thick filament centered during contraction (reviewed in Chauveau et al., 2014; Linke and Hamdani, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Titin acts as a molecular spring responsible for passive force in striated muscle.
source: Titin is the largest known protein and stretches from the Z-line to the M-band, acting as a molecular spring responsible for passive force in striated muscle and for keeping the thick filament centered during contraction (reviewed in Chauveau et al., 2014; Linke and Hamdani, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Titin is responsible for keeping the thick filament centered during contraction.
source: Titin is the largest known protein and stretches from the Z-line to the M-band, acting as a molecular spring responsible for passive force in striated muscle and for keeping the thick filament centered during contraction (reviewed in Chauveau et al., 2014; Linke and Hamdani, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Titin is essential for sarcomere assembly and organization.
source: Titin is essential for sarcomere assembly and organization and plays an important role in mechanosensing and force transmission at the Z-line.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Titin plays an important role in mechanosensing and force transmission at the Z-line.
source: Titin is essential for sarcomere assembly and organization and plays an important role in mechanosensing and force transmission at the Z-line.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The direct and indirect binding of MYPN to titin, its dual localization, and the maladaptive response of MKO mice to biomechanical stress point to a possible role of MYPN in mechano-dependent signaling.
source: The direct as well as indirect binding of MYPN to titin, its dual localization in the sarcomere and the nucleus, and the maladaptive response of MKO mice to biomechanical stress point to a possible role of MYPN in mechano-dependent signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the collective findings.

claim: The function of MYPN in the nucleus is unknown.
source: However, the function of MYPN in the nucleus is unknown and the exact mechanism by which MYPN would transmit biomechanical stress to the nucleus remains to be discovered.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: MYPN likely plays mainly a structural role and its absence weakens the Z-line.
source: Although ultrastructural studies and immunostainings showed normal sarcomere structure, another, more likely, possibility is that MYPN plays mainly a structural role and that its absence weakens the Z-line, where it binds to α-actinin (Bang et al., 2001), nebulette (Bang et al., 2001), titin, and PDZ-LIM family members (von Nandelstadh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the binding partners and phenotype.

claim: MKO skeletal muscle shows progressive Z-line widening with age.
source: In support of this, we recently found progressive Z-line widening with age and eccentric contraction-induced Z-line abnormalities after downhill running in MKO skeletal muscle (Filomena et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: MKO skeletal muscle shows eccentric contraction-induced Z-line abnormalities after downhill running.
source: In support of this, we recently found progressive Z-line widening with age and eccentric contraction-induced Z-line abnormalities after downhill running in MKO skeletal muscle (Filomena et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: MYPN plays an important role for the maintenance of Z-line integrity in skeletal muscle during aging and exercise.
source: demonstrating the important role of MYPN for the maintenance of Z-line integrity in skeletal muscle during aging and exercise.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the skeletal muscle phenotype data cited.

claim: MKO mice have reduced myofiber cross-sectional area in skeletal muscle.
source: In our recent study of the skeletal muscle phenotype of MKO mice, we found that MKO mice have a reduced myofiber cross-sectional area in skeletal muscle and consequently show decreased isometric force and power output as a result of reduced SRF signaling (Filomena et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: MKO mice show decreased isometric force and power output in skeletal muscle as a result of reduced SRF signaling.
source: In our recent study of the skeletal muscle phenotype of MKO mice, we found that MKO mice have a reduced myofiber cross-sectional area in skeletal muscle and consequently show decreased isometric force and power output as a result of reduced SRF signaling (Filomena et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous publication by the authors.

claim: The SRF pathway is regulated by actin dynamics.
source: The SRF pathway is regulated by actin dynamics as its activation is dependent on the nuclear translocation of its cofactor MRTF-A, which is sequestered in the cytosol through binding to globular actin and released upon actin polymerization (Olson and Nordheim, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: MYPN binds and bundles F-actin.
source: We demonstrated that MYPN binds and bundles F-actin as well as interacts with MRTF-A, thereby affecting actin dynamics and consequently the SRF pathway.
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: MYPN interacts with MRTF-A.
source: We demonstrated that MYPN binds and bundles F-actin as well as interacts with MRTF-A, thereby affecting actin dynamics and consequently the SRF pathway.
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous publication by the authors.

claim: MYPN affects actin dynamics and consequently the SRF pathway.
source: We demonstrated that MYPN binds and bundles F-actin as well as interacts with MRTF-A, thereby affecting actin dynamics and consequently the SRF pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism based on previous findings.

claim: The SRF pathway does not appear to be affected in MKO heart.
source: In contrast to skeletal muscle, the SRF pathway does not appear to be affected in MKO heart as there was no downregulation of known SRF target genes
evidence: This conclusion is based on the qRT-PCR data in Figure 6.

claim: Nppa, Nppb, Acta1, Actc1, Myh6, Myh7, and Ankrd1 are known SRF target genes.
source: such as Nppa, Nppb, Acta1, Actc1, Myh6, Myh7, and Ankrd1 (reported in the Harmonizome database; under 'ENCODE Transcription Factor Targets'; https://amp.pharm.mssm.edu/Harmonizome/gene_set/).
evidence: This is stated with reference to a database.

claim: After TAC, Nppa, Nppb, Actc1, Myh7, and Ankrd1 were significantly more upregulated in MKO mice compared to WT mice.
source: In fact, after TAC, Nppa, Nppb, Actc1, Myh7, and Ankrd1, which are markers of biomechanical stress, were significantly more upregulated in MKO mice compared to WT mice
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 6 show higher expression of these genes in MKO mice after TAC.

claim: Nppa, Nppb, Actc1, Myh7, and Ankrd1 are markers of biomechanical stress.
source: In fact, after TAC, Nppa, Nppb, Actc1, Myh7, and Ankrd1, which are markers of biomechanical stress
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The pathological response of MKO mice to TAC does not appear to be directly related to alterations in the SRF pathway.
source: Thus, the pathological response of MKO mice to TAC does not appear to be directly related to alterations in the SRF pathway.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the gene expression data.

claim: Western blot analyses showed no differences in expression of MYPN-interacting proteins between WT and MKO mice.
source: Western blot analyses for the expression of MYPN-interacting proteins and activation of cardiac signaling pathways showed no differences between WT and MKO mice.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6K show no significant differences.

claim: Western blot analyses showed no differences in activation of cardiac signaling pathways between WT and MKO mice.
source: Western blot analyses for the expression of MYPN-interacting proteins and activation of cardiac signaling pathways showed no differences between WT and MKO mice.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 6K show no significant differences in phosphorylation of signaling proteins.

claim: SORBS2 is an adaptor protein located at the adherens junction of the ICD and the Z-line.
source: SORBS2 is an adaptor protein located at the adherens junction of the ICD and the Z-line (Ding et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: SORBS2 interacts with F-actin, α-actinin, and PALLD.
source: where it interacts with a variety of cytoskeletal proteins, including F-actin, α-actinin, and PALLD (Rönty et al., 2005; Sanger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: SORBS2 has been reported to be upregulated in patients with left ventricular noncompaction cardiomyopathy.
source: SORBS2 has been reported to be upregulated in patients with left ventricular noncompaction cardiomyopathy (Li et al., 2020) and heart failure (Vigil-Garcia et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: SORBS2 has been reported to be upregulated in patients with heart failure.
source: SORBS2 has been reported to be upregulated in patients with left ventricular noncompaction cardiomyopathy (Li et al., 2020) and heart failure (Vigil-Garcia et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: AAV9-mediated SORBS2 overexpression in mouse heart resulted in microtubule densification, T-tubule disorganization, defective Ca2+ handling, and cardiac systolic dysfunction.
source: Adeno-associated virus 9-mediated overexpression in mouse heart resulted in microtubule densification, T-tubule disorganization, defective Ca2+ handling, and cardiac systolic dysfunction (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Reduced Ca2+ amplitude and prolonged TTP and time to decay of the Ca2+ transient were observed in isolated cardiomyocytes from SORBS2 overexpressing mice.
source: In particular, reduced Ca2+ amplitude and prolonged TTP and time to decay of the Ca2+ transient were observed in isolated CMCs from SORBS2 overexpressing mice, similar to what we observed in MKO mice
evidence: This is stated with a citation and compared to the current findings.

claim: The altered Ca2+ handling in MKO mice may be at least partly explained by the upregulation of SORBS2.
source: suggesting that the altered Ca2+ handling in MKO mice may be at least partly explained by the upregulation of SORBS2.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the SORBS2 upregulation to the Ca2+ handling phenotype.

claim: The upregulation of SORBS2 in MKO mice may be related to alterations in the actin cytoskeleton due to the absence of MYPN.
source: Since both SORBS2 and MYPN are tightly associated with the actin cytoskeleton, it is possible that the upregulation of SORBS2 in MKO mice is related to alterations in the actin cytoskeleton due to the absence of MYPN.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the known functions of these proteins.

claim: Increased expression of ICD proteins and higher ICD fold amplitude are commonly associated with the pathology of DCM.
source: Furthermore, increased expression of ICD proteins and higher ICD fold amplitude are commonly associated with the pathology of DCM (Ortega et al., 2017; Perriard et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The upregulation of SORBS2 and desmoplakin may be related to the DCM phenotype of MKO mice.
source: so the upregulation of SORBS2 and desmoplakin may be related to the DCM phenotype of MKO mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the protein changes to the phenotype.

claim: CASQ2 is a Ca2+-binding protein located in the lumen of the SR.
source: CASQ2 is a Ca2+-binding protein located in the lumen of the SR, where it acts as a Ca2+ buffer and an inhibitory modulator of SR Ca2+ release by regulation of RyR2 to prevent premature spontaneous SR Ca2+ release during conditions of high SR Ca2+ load (Chopra et al., 2007; Knollmann et al., 2006; Song et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: CASQ2 acts as a Ca2+ buffer and an inhibitory modulator of SR Ca2+ release by regulation of RyR2.
source: CASQ2 is a Ca2+-binding protein located in the lumen of the SR, where it acts as a Ca2+ buffer and an inhibitory modulator of SR Ca2+ release by regulation of RyR2 to prevent premature spontaneous SR Ca2+ release during conditions of high SR Ca2+ load (Chopra et al., 2007; Knollmann et al., 2006; Song et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: CASQ2 is a known interaction partner of CARP.
source: CASQ2 is a known interaction partner of CARP, although CARP has not been detected in the SR, but it was suggested that CASQ2 is present in the cytoplasm at low levels, allowing for the interaction to take place (Torrado et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: MYPN may be indirectly linked to CASQ2 through CARP.
source: MYPN may thus be indirectly linked to CASQ2 through CARP.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known interactions.

claim: The downregulation of CASQ2 in MKO mice at the early stage after TAC is most likely a secondary effect of the alterations due to MYPN ablation and SORBS2 upregulation.
source: However, we consider it most likely that the downregulation of CASQ2 in MKO mice at the early stage after TAC is a secondary effect of the alterations due to MYPN ablation and SORBS2 upregulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Reduction of CASQ2 levels in cardiomyocytes results in reduced twitch Ca2+ transient amplitude and duration as a result of decreased Ca2+ SR content.
source: A reduction of CASQ2 levels in CMCs has been reported to result in reduced twitch Ca2+ transient amplitude and duration as a result of decreased Ca2+ SR content (Terentyev et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: CASQ2 reduction in cardiomyocytes results in reduced Ca2+ spark amplitude and duration.
source: Furthermore, Ca2+ spark amplitude and duration were reduced, while Ca2+ spark frequency and velocity of Ca2+ release were unaffected (Terentyev et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: CASQ2 deficiency or reduction in mouse had only minor effects on SR Ca2+ content, Ca2+ transients, and contractile function under basal conditions.
source: In contrast, CASQ2 deficiency or reduction in mouse had only minor effects on SR Ca2+ content, Ca2+ transients, and contractile function under basal conditions (Chopra et al., 2007; Knollmann et al., 2006; Song et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Isoproterenol stimulation caused increased SR Ca2+ leak in CASQ2-deficient mice.
source: However, while diastolic SR Ca2+ leak (Ca2+ spark frequency) was unaltered at basal levels, isoproterenol stimulation caused increased SR Ca2+ leak, making CASQ2-deficient mice more susceptible to stress-induced ventricular arrhythmias.
evidence: This is stated with implicit citations to the previous sentence.

claim: CASQ2-deficient mice are more susceptible to stress-induced ventricular arrhythmias.
source: making CASQ2-deficient mice more susceptible to stress-induced ventricular arrhythmias.
evidence: This is stated with implicit citations to the previous sentence.

claim: Differences between acute and chronic CASQ2 reduction may explain the different consequences of CASQ2 modulation in vitro and in vivo.
source: Differences between acute (CMCs) and chronic CASQ2 reduction (knockout mice) may explain the different consequences of CASQ2 modulation in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation to reconcile different findings.

claim: The reduced Ca2+ spark amplitude and width as well as increased Ca2+ spark TTP in cardiomyocytes from MKO mice 7 days after TAC may be explained by the reduced CASQ2 levels.
source: The reduced Ca2+ spark amplitude and width as well as increased Ca2+ spark TTP in CMCs from MKO mice 7 days after TAC are consistent with the published observations in CMCs with reduced CASQ2 levels (Terentyev et al., 2003), and may thus be explained by the reduced CASQ2 levels in MKO mice 4 days after TAC.
evidence: This interpretation connects the Ca2+ spark data with the CASQ2 data and published findings.

claim: The alterations in Ca2+ handling under basal conditions in MKO mice are likely unrelated to CASQ2.
source: On the other hand, the alterations under basal conditions, including prolonged Ca2+ transient TTP and time to decay as well as increased Ca2+ spark time to decay to levels comparable to those of WT mice after TAC are likely unrelated to CASQ2 as CASQ2 levels were unaltered under basal conditions.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the lack of CASQ2 changes at baseline.

claim: The reduced velocity of Ca2+ release from the SR in MKO mice may be related to the upregulation of SORBS2.
source: The same applies for the velocity of Ca2+ release from the SR, which was reduced both under basal conditions and after TAC. These changes may instead be related to the upregulation of SORBS2 as discussed above.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the Ca2+ release velocity to SORBS2.

claim: Delayed Ca2+ release and reuptake are typical signs of heart failure.
source: Delayed Ca2+ release and reuptake are typical signs of heart failure (Roe et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Delayed Ca2+ release and reuptake have been linked to slowed Ca2+ spark kinetics due to reorganization of RyR2 clusters.
source: and have been linked to slowed Ca2+ spark kinetics due to reorganization of RyR2 clusters (Kolstad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Altered Ca2+ handling likely contributes to the development of DCM in MKO mice.
source: Thus, as these alterations happen before the manifestation of cardiac dysfunction in MKO mice, altered Ca2+ handling likely contributes to the development of DCM in MKO mice.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the temporal relationship between Ca2+ handling changes and cardiac dysfunction.

claim: Human heterozygous MYPN gene mutations have been associated with HCM, DCM, and RCM.
source: Human heterozygous MYPN gene mutations have been associated with HCM, DCM, and RCM (Bagnall et al., 2010; Duboscq-Bidot et al., 2008; Meyer et al., 2013; Purevjav et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Transgenic mice overexpressing the MYPN-Y20C variant developed HCM and severely disrupted ICDs.
source: MYPN-Y20C transgenic mice developed HCM and severely disrupted ICDs, associated with impaired binding of MYPN to CARP, reduced CARP protein levels, and failure of MYPN-Y20C to translocate to the nucleus (Purevjav et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: The physiological significance of findings in MYPN-Y20C transgenic mice is unclear due to high overexpression levels.
source: However, since MYPN-Y20C was overexpressed at high levels, the physiological significance of these findings is unclear.
evidence: This is a critical interpretation of the cited study.

claim: Heterozygous MYPN-Q529X knockin mice developed RCM characterized by diastolic dysfunction and interstitial and perivascular fibrosis.
source: Heterozygous MYPN-Q529X knockin mice expressed a truncated 65 kDa peptide in the nucleus and developed RCM, characterized by diastolic dysfunction and interstitial and perivascular fibrosis (Huby et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Heterozygous MYPN-Q529X knockin mice showed decreased CARP protein levels and reduced phosphorylation of Erk1/2, Smad2, and Akt.
source: This was associated with decreased protein levels of CARP as well as reduced phosphorylation levels of Erk1/2, Smad2, and Akt, while protein levels of nebulette, desmin, and MLP/Csrp3 were increased.
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Homozygous MYPN-Q526X knockin mice had barely detectable MYPN-Q526X levels due to nonsense-mediated mRNA instability.
source: In contrast, homozygous MYPN-Q526X knockin mice had barely detectable MYPN-Q526X levels as a result of nonsense-mediated mRNA instability and showed no discernable cardiac alterations
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Homozygous MYPN-Q526X knockin mice showed no discernable cardiac alterations.
source: In contrast, homozygous MYPN-Q526X knockin mice had barely detectable MYPN-Q526X levels as a result of nonsense-mediated mRNA instability and showed no discernable cardiac alterations, although the mice were not studied under conditions of stress (Huby et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation.

claim: Cardiomyopathy-associated MYPN mutations are thought to have dominant negative effects.
source: Thus, the cardiomyopathy-associated MYPN mutations are thought to have dominant negative effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison of heterozygous and homozygous mouse models.

claim: Homozygous MYPN-Q526X knockin mice would likely develop cardiac systolic dysfunction with age or in response to stress.
source: Since MKO mice show a relatively mild form of slowly progressive DCM under basal conditions and MYPN-Q526X knockin mice were only studied until 12 weeks of age, it is likely that the phenotype was missed and that homozygous MYPN-Q526X knockin mice, like MKO mice, would develop cardiac systolic dysfunction with age or in response to stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the MKO phenotype and the limited study duration of the knockin mice.

claim: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in MYPN have been identified in patients with nemaline myopathy, cap myopathy, and congenital myopathy with hanging big toe.
source: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in MYPN have recently been identified in patients with nemaline myopathy (Miyatake et al., 2017), cap myopathy (Lornage et al., 2017), and congenital myopathy with hanging big toe (Merlini et al., 2019), some of which had mild cardiac involvement.
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Some patients with biallelic MYPN mutations had mild cardiac involvement.
source: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in MYPN have recently been identified in patients with nemaline myopathy (Miyatake et al., 2017), cap myopathy (Lornage et al., 2017), and congenital myopathy with hanging big toe (Merlini et al., 2019), some of which had mild cardiac involvement.
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: No patient with biallelic MYPN mutations developed DCM.
source: Although no patient developed DCM, this is consistent with the relatively weak cardiac phenotype of MKO mice under basal conditions.
evidence: This observation is stated and interpreted in the context of the MKO phenotype.

claim: Patients with biallelic MYPN mutations may be more prone to develop cardiac disease in response to cardiovascular risk factors.
source: The maladaptive response of MKO mice to pressure overload suggests that these patients may be more prone to develop cardiac disease in response to cardiovascular risk factors, such as hypertension, obesity, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, etc.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the mouse model to human patients.

claim: The results highlight the importance of periodic monitoring of heart function in patients with biallelic MYPN mutations.
source: Thus, our results highlight the importance of periodic monitoring of heart function in these patients and the need to reduce cardiovascular risk factors by encouraging healthy life style choices and timely therapeutic management.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: There is a need to reduce cardiovascular risk factors in patients with biallelic MYPN mutations by encouraging healthy lifestyle choices and timely therapeutic management.
source: Thus, our results highlight the importance of periodic monitoring of heart function in these patients and the need to reduce cardiovascular risk factors by encouraging healthy life style choices and timely therapeutic management.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on the study findings.
